questions.q: What is the key difference between standard TLS and mutual TLS (mTLS)?
options: Standard TLS only proves the server's identity to the client; mTLS also requires the client to present a certificate the server validates
mTLS does not encrypt traffic, while standard TLS does
Standard TLS is only usable for inbound connections, and mTLS only for outbound
There is no real difference; they are two names for the same protocol
questions.explain: Standard TLS is one-way trust: the client checks the server's certificate. mTLS adds the missing half -- the server also validates a certificate from the client before the connection is considered authenticated.

questions.q: In the JWT Bearer flow, what does Salesforce actually need in order to validate the integration's signed token?
options: The integration's private key, which Salesforce stores securely
A copy of the integration's password
The matching certificate uploaded to the connected app ahead of time, which lets Salesforce check the signature without ever seeing the private key
Nothing; JWT Bearer flow performs no validation at all
questions.explain: Salesforce validates the JWT's signature against the public certificate uploaded to the connected app. The private key never leaves the system that holds it, which is exactly what makes certificate-based auth stronger than a shared secret.

questions.q: If an integration's private key used for the JWT Bearer flow is compromised, what does this lesson say has to happen to rotate it?
options: Every Salesforce user's password must be reset org-wide
A new key pair must be generated and the new certificate uploaded -- it does not involve resetting anyone's password
Nothing can be done; the connected app must be deleted and recreated from scratch
The org must switch permanently to the Username-Password flow
questions.explain: Because the trust anchor is a certificate rather than a password, rotation means generating a new key pair and uploading the new certificate -- it's a credential swap for the integration, unrelated to any human user's password.

questions.q: Why does this lesson warn against using a self-signed certificate for a production integration?
options: Self-signed certificates are always technically invalid and will never work anywhere
The receiving system has no trusted certificate authority to validate it against, and different platforms vary in whether they'll accept it -- some reject it outright
Self-signed certificates cannot encrypt traffic
Salesforce charges extra for any integration using a self-signed certificate
questions.explain: A self-signed certificate has no CA backing it, so a receiving system has no established trust path to validate it against. Behavior varies by platform/feature, which is exactly why the lesson recommends verifying against current docs and defaulting to a CA-signed certificate for production.

questions.q: This lesson says certificates and mTLS solve identity and encryption but NOT authorization. What does that mean in practice?
options: A validly certificate-authenticated caller can still be over-privileged if the identity behind that certificate has more access than the integration needs
Certificates make authorization checks unnecessary, since identity verification is sufficient on its own
mTLS automatically restricts a caller to the minimum access needed
Authorization only matters for human users, never for certificate-authenticated integrations
questions.explain: Certificates answer 'is this really who it claims to be,' not 'should this caller be allowed to do what it's asking to do.' A certificate-authenticated connection tied to an over-privileged identity is just as risky as any other over-privileged integration -- authorization scoping is a separate job, covered in Lessons 5 and 6.
